status: NOT USABLE -- the three B2 zero-shot cases have been retrained on the repaired caches and still do not learn. No B2 zero-shot number is admissible.
why_this_file_exists: INVALID_B2_zeroshot.json records why the ORIGINAL three B2 eval reports are invalid (a mesh-dependent load overstatement). It ends with 'retrain all three B2 cases on the repaired caches'. That was done. This file records the outcome, so that the next session does not re-derive it or assume the retrain fixed it.

what_was_run.protocol: identical to the three B1 zero-shot cases -- geometry B2, train_resolutions 21,33, 400 train and 100 val per resolution, 2000 epochs, validate_every 25, batch_size 8
what_was_run.difference_from_the_first_attempt: --loss_force_norm on. It was missing from this trainer entirely and was added first; report section 9.1 established that once B2's boundary force is FEM-consistent the loss must be divided by the per-sample force scale, and that correcting the force WITHOUT it took B2 from 32.46% to 94.08%.

result.shape: best at essentially the first validation and worse afterwards in all three; early stopping fired in all three
result.for_comparison: the three B1 cases under the same trainer and the same protocol reach 0.0658 to 0.0827 on the same metric, and 0.050 to 0.106 on the eval metric
result.eval_note: an earlier revision of this file said '0.87 to 0.89, flat in the mesh to the fourth decimal'. The range is right; 'to the fourth decimal' is not. Neo-Hookean moves in the third (0.87137 to 0.87270). The accurate statement is that each B2 curve varies by less than 0.2% across the same fourfold refinement over which the three B1 curves vary by 79% to 111% (NH 86%, MR 111%, AB 79%). An error that ignores the mesh is the signature of a model that is not solving the problem on that mesh.

why_1_point_0_is_the_number_to_notice: the metric is 0.5*(rms(e_u)/rms(u) + rms(e_v)/rms(v)); substitute uv_pred = 0 and it is identically 1. A model sitting at 1.0 is predicting approximately nothing. That is not necessarily an optimiser failure: a network that minimises Pi goes wherever Pi's minimum is, so the question is whether Pi's minimum, built from this cache's node_forces, is anywhere near this cache's uv_exact.

candidates_tested.candidate: loss_force_norm missing from the zero-shot trainer
candidates_tested.verdict: NECESSARY BUT NOT SUFFICIENT -- it was added and the retrain above is with it on

candidates_tested.candidate: batch size. b2_accuracy_search.py's 'lossnorm' trial reached 9.11% on B2 x Neo-Hookean calling train_B2.py at its default batch size of ONE, while this trainer defaults to eight
candidates_tested.test: two arms on B2 x Neo-Hookean at MATCHED optimizer steps (22,400, a multiple of both arms' steps-per-epoch), early stopping off so both ran the full budget
candidates_tested.verdict: NOT THE CAUSE -- 0.9444 against 0.9888 is noise on curves that swing between 0.94 and 1.45, and neither is anywhere near the 0.07 B1 reaches

candidates_tested.candidate: Pi's minimum is not at the true solution for this cache -- i.e. the data and the functional disagree, and the trainer is finding zero correctly
candidates_tested.test: omar_pfem/test_b2_zeroshot_functional.py -- Pi(s * uv_exact) scanned over s, no training needed
candidates_tested.verdict: RULED OUT -- the data and the functional AGREE. Pi(s * uv_exact) was scanned over s on 3 samples at each of the two training resolutions and the minimum landed at s = 1.0 in all 6, with no exceptions and no spread.

measured.why_that_number_matters: for a stationary point of Pi = U - W in a problem whose stored energy is quadratic to leading order, W = 2U. Getting 2.00 to three decimals on six independent samples is a second, independent confirmation that uv_exact is the minimiser of this Pi and not merely close to it.
measured.the_curve_is_flat_near_the_minimum: Pi(0.85) and Pi(1.15) sit about 2% of |Pi| above Pi(1.0), so a 15% amplitude error costs almost nothing in the objective. That does not explain a factor of ten, but it is worth stating when reading how hard the objective pushes on amplitude.

candidates_tested.candidate: the training path itself: the model's input channels, or its ability to descend at all
candidates_tested.why_this_is_what_is_left: the cache, the work term and the functional are now excluded by measurement, and the optimiser settings tried (force normalisation, batch size) are excluded by experiment. What remains is what the model is fed and what it does with it.
candidates_tested.the_specific_suspicion: fun_material is (E, nu, f_x, f_y) fed RAW -- there is no normalisation anywhere in train_B2's energy function, which the zero-shot trainer re-exports unchanged. For B2 the load is an inner-edge traction, so f is exactly zero on every node off that boundary (about 95% of them at N=21), and the load repair made what remains 13-21x smaller. E is around 1000. If the two channels carrying the loading are orders of magnitude below the one carrying stiffness and nonzero on a twentieth of the nodes, the model may not see the load at all -- which would give an error flat in N, flat across materials, and stuck near 1.0. This is a suspicion and is not yet measured.
candidates_tested.a_second_difference_worth_naming: the 9.11% recipe and this study are not on the same problem family. data_generate_B2.py draws (E, nu, p) from a 2-D Gaussian random field in (theta, r); the zero-shot study uses ParametricFieldB2, a two-harmonic Fourier series in theta ALONE, chosen because it is resolution-independent by construction and a gridded GRF is not. So '9.11% is reachable on B2' was never transferable evidence about this trainer. B1 uses the same kind of parametric field and trains fine, so this is not on its own an explanation either.
candidates_tested.test: omar_pfem/test_b2_zeroshot_model.py -- prints the input channel scales as fed, what the trained model predicts (rms ratio and correlation), Pi at that prediction, and how much the prediction changes across samples on one mesh. No training.
candidates_tested.verdict: PARTLY MEASURED -- the model is not ignoring its input, but it responds about five times too weakly and emits a field of nearly fixed strain energy whatever it is shown. Not yet a cause.

first_probe_2026_08_31.run: B2 x Neo-Hookean, 4 val samples at each of N=21 and N=33, CPU, commit c7f63c6
first_probe_2026_08_31.not_predicting_zero: rms(pred) 2.512e-03 to 3.344e-03 against targets 4.148e-03 to 1.280e-02. So the 1.0 error is not a dead model.
first_probe_2026_08_31.and_that_is_the_important_one: W/U = 2 is the stationarity condition under rescaling. The prediction already satisfies it to within a few tens of per cent, so the model is NOT part-way down a ray with more to go: rescaling its output would not recover the solution. Its shape is wrong, not merely its size. Note the tension with the amplitude ratio -- if the prediction were s*uv_exact, W/U = 2/s would imply s = 0.6 to 1.1, against the 0.23 to 0.61 measured, which is itself proof the prediction does not lie on the solution ray.

U_at_the_prediction_is_nearly_constant.spread: 1.42x across all eight samples and BOTH meshes
U_at_the_prediction_is_nearly_constant.against: the targets' rms spans 3.09x, and Pi(uv_exact) on the train samples spanned 10x
U_at_the_prediction_is_nearly_constant.reading: the model emits a field of nearly fixed strain energy whatever sample it is shown. That is the collapse, measured in the most physical variable available.

it_does_read_its_input_but_too_weakly.reading: about a fifth to a third of the variation it should show. So 'ignoring the fields entirely' is ruled out, and 'responding far too weakly' is what replaces it.

two_faults_in_the_probe_itself: it reported Pi(pred) with no Pi(uv_exact) for the SAME sample. The functional test's Pi values are on train_samples and the probe reads val_samples, which are different problems, so Pi(pred) could not be compared with anything. Fixed: both are now computed per sample and what is printed is the fraction of the available descent.

it printed the channel scales at N=21 and N=33 side by side as though the difference were a mesh effect. It is not separable that way -- the cache uses seed_base = 10_000 * N, so those are different DRAWS as well as different meshes. Fixed: one fixed seed is rebuilt on both meshes, and the mesh-independent load total is printed beside the per-node scale.
candidates_tested.and_the_control_that_was_missing: B1 reaches 0.066 on the same trainer, the same architecture and the same protocol. Any account of B2's failure that would apply equally to B1 explains nothing. The probe now runs both arms and prints them together.

what_is_safe_to_say_in_the_report: the caches were repaired and the repair verified mesh-independent; all three cases were retrained under the B1 protocol with the force normalisation section 9.1 requires; the retrained models sit at a combined validation error of about 1.0, which is what predicting zero scores; the cause is under investigation and is not the optimiser settings tried so far.
provenance: the three training histories and the three eval reports were read directly from Drive on 2026-08-31 (pfem_run/zeroshot_B2_*/metrics_history.json and zeroshot_eval_coarse_and_fine.json) and every number in this file matches them. The batch-size arms were read from pfem_run/b2_batchsize_diagnostic/bs{1,8}/metrics_history.json: bs8 best 0.98880 at epoch 18 (1,800 steps), bs1 best 0.94436 at epoch 6 (4,800 steps), both arms run out to 22,400 optimizer steps with early stopping off.
